analysis.one_liner: Doubles the number of prescription drugs Medicare negotiates prices for and starts sooner.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate prices for 20 drugs in 2026 and 40 a year after — instead of 10 and 15 — died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Inflation Reduction Act let Medicare negotiate prices for a small, slowly growing list of expensive brand-name drugs. This bill would have roughly doubled that list starting in 2026, let drugs become eligible for negotiation after only 3 years on the market instead of 9 to 13, tightened the caps on the negotiated prices, and repealed a rule that bars Medicare officials from taking part in drug price discussions. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. More of the costliest brand-name drugs would face negotiated maximum prices, sooner, which is projected to lower out-of-pocket costs for seniors and reduce what Medicare pays from the federal budget.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for 20 drugs in 2026 and 40 drugs per year thereafter, instead of the 10-15-20 schedule under current law [S2] [S3].
Shortens the time a drug must be on the market before it can be negotiated — from 7 years for drugs and 11 years for biologics down to 3 years for both [S2] [S3].
Tightens the price ceilings for the negotiated 'maximum fair price' (for example, lowering the long-monopoly ceiling from 40 percent to 30 percent of a benchmark price) [S2] [S3].
Repeals the Part D 'noninterference clause' that bars Medicare officials from intervening in price negotiations between drug makers, pharmacies, and Part D plan sponsors [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which would face more drugs being negotiated earlier, lower price ceilings, and a government that can engage directly in price discussions. Some of that cost could be offset by manufacturers raising launch prices on new drugs outside the negotiation program.

drawbacks.text: The negotiation program already contains an excise-tax penalty for drug makers that refuse to negotiate, and expanding it further could lead manufacturers to raise the introductory prices of new drugs that are not yet eligible, which would hit patients before negotiation applies — a tradeoff the bill text does not address [S3].

Negotiating 40 drugs a year and making drugs eligible after only 3 years is a major expansion of government price-setting; drug makers argue shorter market exclusivity reduces revenue available to reinvest in new medicines, which supporters of current law cite as a reason for the longer timelines [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare patients and the federal budget the benefits are concrete: lower prices on more drugs, sooner. The main cost is borne by brand-name drug companies and possibly by future patients through higher launch prices for new drugs, a tradeoff opponents of the IRA's expansion frequently raise. The bill never got a hearing or a vote, so its design was never tested or refined in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day and never moved — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the SMART Prices Act on April 20, 2023, with 24 original cosponsors [S1].
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; no further action was ever taken [S5].
It gathered 29 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, but was never reported out of the Finance Committee [S4] [S5].

The bill would have expanded the Medicare drug price negotiation program created by the Inflation Reduction Act: 20 drugs negotiated in 2026 and 40 per year thereafter, eligibility after 3 years instead of 7-11, lower price ceilings, and repeal of the noninterference clause [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: none of their most expensive drugs were added to the negotiation list early, market exclusivity stayed at 9-13 years, and the noninterference clause remains in force. Senators who did not act are spared from voting on it.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand and accelerate Medicare drug price negotiation.

for.name: 29 Senate cosponsors
for.role: All Democrats or independents caucusing with Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I) and Sen. Angus King (I), but none had committee tools to move it past Finance.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance leadership
against.role: Committee of referral — never took the bill up
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership and caucus
against.role: No Republican cosponsor; committee majority controls scheduling
against.what_they_did: Offered no support for expanding the IRA drug negotiation program, keeping the bill a Democratic-only measure with no path past committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of brand-name drugs subject to negotiation
against.what_they_did: Opposed expansion of the Medicare negotiation program, which cuts revenue on their most profitable drugs; the industry has lobbied heavily against all such expansions.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill would have doubled the number of their drugs subject to Medicare price negotiation, made drugs eligible after 3 years instead of 9-13, and cut the price ceilings, reducing revenue on their most profitable products. The bill's death preserves the slower IRA timeline and their market exclusivity.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Repealing the noninterference clause would let Medicare officials intervene in price negotiations between manufacturers, pharmacies, and plan sponsors, changing their negotiating position, but the practical effect on their bottom line is indirect and uncertain.
More drugs negotiated sooner means lower out-of-pocket costs for seniors and lower Medicare spending borne by taxpayers. This is a public stake, listed for completeness.
